title: What an eval set is
question: In LLM application development, what is an evaluation (eval) set?
options: A collection of representative inputs paired with expected outputs or grading criteria, reused to score every change
A single hand-picked prompt that the team re-reads after each release to decide whether the model still feels right overall
The portion of the model's original training corpus that the provider reserves for measuring accuracy of its own base weights
A log of all production conversations stored as-is, replayed to users so that they can rate each answer manually afterwards
explanation: An eval set gives you a repeatable, comparable measurement: the same representative cases are run after each prompt, model or retrieval change. A single prompt is anecdotal, the provider's internal held-out training data is not available to you, and a raw conversation log has no expected outputs or criteria to score against.

title: Defining success criteria
question: Before building evals for an LLM feature, what should the success criteria look like?
options: Broad goals such as "the assistant should feel helpful and natural", reviewed by the team during each demo session
Specific and measurable targets, such as an F1 score on a labeled set or at least 95% of answers passing a rubric
Whatever the first working prototype happens to produce, since later changes are then compared against that baseline output
A single accuracy figure on one dataset, chosen to ignore latency, cost and safety so the number stays easy to explain
explanation: Good criteria are specific and measurable so that a change can be judged better or worse without debate. Vague goals cannot be scored, defining success from whatever the prototype outputs bakes in its flaws, and a single accuracy number ignores latency, cost and safety, which usually matter in production too.

title: Edge cases in an eval set
question: Which addition makes an eval set for a support chatbot more trustworthy?
options: Many paraphrases of the same easy question so the pass rate stays high and the dashboard looks healthy to stakeholders
Only questions the team already knows the current prompt answers well, to avoid noisy failures that block each release
Hard and unusual inputs such as typos, ambiguous requests, off-topic questions and attempts to break the rules
Exactly the examples already placed in the prompt as few-shot demonstrations, because the model has already seen them
explanation: An eval set should cover the range of real traffic, including the rare and difficult inputs where failures hide. Repeating easy paraphrases or choosing only passing cases inflates the score without finding problems, and reusing the few-shot examples tests memorized demonstrations instead of generalization.

title: Choosing a grading method
question: Which grading method is the fastest and most reliable for questions with one exact expected answer, such as a category label?
options: Having a person read every output each time, because human judgement is always the most consistent grader available
Asking an LLM judge for an overall quality score from one to ten, because numeric scales are precise for any task
Counting the characters in each answer and comparing the total with the length of the reference answer for that case
Code-based grading, such as exact string match, since it is deterministic, instant and costs nothing per run
explanation: When the answer is one exact value, a program can compare it with the expected label deterministically, instantly and for free. Human review is slow and varies between reviewers, an LLM judge adds cost and variance where none is needed, and character counts say nothing about correctness.

title: Jailbreak versus prompt injection
question: How does OWASP relate jailbreaking to prompt injection?
options: They are unrelated: jailbreaking only concerns network attacks against the hosting servers, never the model's instructions or behavior
Jailbreaking is a form of prompt injection in which the input makes the model ignore its safety rules
Prompt injection only exists in image models, while jailbreaking is the equivalent attack for text-only language models
They are identical names for exceeding a provider's rate limits by sending too many requests in a short time window
explanation: OWASP treats jailbreaking as a type of prompt injection: crafted input leads the model to disregard its safety protocols or guidelines. Neither term is a network attack, neither is limited to a modality, and neither refers to rate limits, which belong to a different risk category.

title: Sensitive information disclosure
question: Which practice best reduces the risk of an LLM app revealing other customers' personal data?
options: Telling the model in the system prompt to be careful, since an instruction alone is a guaranteed barrier against leaks
Using a larger model, because bigger models never repeat any detail they received in context or in training data
Keeping each user's data scoped by access control and sanitizing or removing sensitive fields before they reach the model
Hiding the model's name from the interface, so that attackers cannot tell which provider is answering their questions
explanation: The reliable defense is data minimization and access control: only data the current user may see should enter the context, and sensitive fields should be stripped or masked first. A polite instruction is not an enforcement mechanism, model size does not prevent leaks, and hiding the provider name does nothing about what the model can reveal.

title: Data poisoning
question: What is data poisoning in the context of LLM security?
options: Overloading the inference endpoint with so many requests that legitimate users are left waiting for responses
Stealing the model weights from a server by copying the files directly from its storage volume
Tricking the user interface into rendering a hidden script that runs in the browser of the person chatting
Planting malicious or biased data in training, fine-tuning or retrieval sources so the model learns harmful behavior
explanation: Poisoning manipulates the data a model learns from or retrieves (pre-training, fine-tuning, embeddings or knowledge bases), introducing backdoors, bias or wrong facts. Request flooding is a denial-of-service issue, copying weights is model theft, and a script rendered in the browser is improper output handling.

title: What LLM APIs bill by
question: What is the usual unit that hosted LLM APIs use to meter and bill usage?
options: Seconds of wall-clock time that the HTTP connection stays open between the client and the provider's servers
The number of distinct users who sent at least one request during the current calendar month
Tokens processed, with input tokens and output tokens commonly priced at different rates
The number of API calls made, regardless of how long the prompt or the generated answer happens to be
explanation: Hosted LLM APIs price by tokens, and output tokens usually cost more than input tokens, so long prompts and long answers both raise the bill. Connection time, monthly active users and raw call count are not how per-request model usage is normally metered.

title: Handling rate-limit errors
question: An LLM API returns HTTP 429 (rate limited) for some requests. What is the standard way for the client to react?
options: Resend the same request immediately in a tight loop until it succeeds, so that no user waits longer than necessary
Treat it as a permanent failure, discard the request and show the user an error without any further attempt
Switch to a random different prompt for the same task, since the limit applies only to prompts that repeat
Retry after a delay that grows exponentially, with some random jitter, and honor any retry hint the API sends
explanation: A 429 is transient, so retrying with exponential backoff and jitter, and respecting a retry-after style hint, lets the limit window recover without piling more load on the service. Hammering immediately makes throttling worse, giving up discards recoverable work, and the limit is not tied to repeated prompts.

title: The context window
question: What does a model's context window limit?
options: The total number of tokens, covering the prompt and the generated output, that the model can handle in a single request
The number of separate users that are allowed to call the same model endpoint at exactly the same moment
The number of requests per minute that an organization may send before the provider starts rejecting them
The amount of time the provider keeps stored conversations before automatically deleting them from its servers
explanation: The context window is the maximum amount of text, measured in tokens, the model can consider at once, including your input and its reply, so long histories must be trimmed or summarized. Concurrency, requests per minute and data retention are separate limits or policies.

title: Open/Closed Principle
question: What does the Open/Closed Principle ask of a well-designed module?
options: It should be open to anyone in the company for edits, and closed only when a release branch is cut
It should be open to new behavior through extension, without editing its existing, tested source code
It should keep every field public so callers can extend it, while methods stay sealed against overriding
It should be closed to all change after the first release, so new needs always require a rewrite
explanation: The principle says software entities should be open for extension but closed for modification: new behavior is added through new code such as another implementation, not by editing proven code. It is not about repository permissions, public fields, or freezing a system after release.

title: Dependency injection versus inversion
question: How does dependency injection relate to the Dependency Inversion Principle?
options: They are two names for the same rule, so any code that injects objects automatically depends on abstractions
Injection forbids the use of interfaces, while inversion requires every class to create its own collaborators
Injection is a runtime technique that only works in dynamically typed languages, unlike the compile-time principle
Injection is a technique that supplies dependencies from outside, helping to apply a principle about depending on abstractions
explanation: Dependency Inversion is the design principle that high-level policy should depend on abstractions, not on concrete details. Dependency injection is one technique, passing collaborators in through constructors or setters, that helps achieve it. Injecting a concrete class still violates the principle, and injection works in typed languages too.

title: Square and Rectangle
question: A `Square` class extends `Rectangle` and overrides `setWidth` so that it also changes the height. Code that sets a width of 5 and a height of 4 on a `Rectangle` expects an area of 20. Which principle does this break?
options: Interface Segregation, because the rectangle exposes more setters than the square needs
Single Responsibility, because the square class both stores dimensions and computes an area
Open/Closed, because adding the square required creating a new class instead of editing the rectangle
Liskov Substitution, because the subtype cannot be used where the base type is expected without surprises
explanation: Liskov Substitution requires that a subtype be usable wherever the base type is expected without breaking its callers' assumptions. A square that couples width and height violates the rectangle's contract, so the area changes unexpectedly. Adding a class is what Open/Closed encourages, and the other principles concern interface size and reasons to change.

title: What cohesion means
question: What does high cohesion mean for a class or module?
options: Its members all work toward one focused purpose and belong together
It imports as many other modules as possible so every feature is reachable from a single place
It has the largest number of lines in the codebase because everything related is kept in a single file
Its fields are all public so that other modules can read and update any of its internal state quickly
explanation: Cohesion measures how strongly the parts of a module relate to one purpose; high cohesion makes it easy to name, understand and change. Importing many modules increases coupling, sheer size often signals low cohesion, and public mutable fields weaken encapsulation rather than improving focus.

title: Reducing coupling
question: Which change reduces coupling between an `OrderService` and the email sending code it uses?
options: Copy the email library's source into `OrderService` so it no longer needs to reference another module
Make `OrderService` depend on a small notification interface that the email code implements
Let `OrderService` read the email class's private fields directly to avoid calling its methods
Move the email credentials into `OrderService` fields so both pieces always change at the same time
explanation: Depending on a narrow interface means `OrderService` knows only a contract, so the email implementation can change or be replaced without touching it. Copying code, reaching into private fields and sharing credentials all make the two pieces know more about each other, which increases coupling.

title: Feature envy smell
question: A method in `Invoice` spends most of its body calling getters on a `Customer` to compute a discount. What is this smell called and what is the usual fix?
options: Shotgun surgery; split the method into several tiny ones spread across all the classes it touches
Primitive obsession; replace the getters with plain numeric values returned by the customer class
Feature envy; move the method, or the part that uses the data, into the `Customer` class
Speculative generality; delete the `Customer` class so that the invoice stores the data itself
explanation: Feature envy appears when a method is more interested in another class's data than its own, which signals low cohesion and high coupling. Moving the behavior next to the data it uses fixes it. Shotgun surgery concerns one change touching many classes, primitive obsession concerns overusing basic types, and speculative generality concerns unused flexibility.

title: The KISS principle
question: What does the KISS principle recommend when two designs both solve the problem?
options: Choose the one with more layers and abstractions, because extra structure always prepares the code for future growth
Choose the one that uses the newest language features, since modern syntax is usually easier for others to read
Choose the one with the shortest possible code, even when it relies on cryptic tricks that few teammates understand
Choose the simpler one that is easy to understand and change, adding complexity only when it is needed
explanation: KISS (keep it simple) favors the simplest design that works, since simple code is easier to read, test and change. Extra layers without a need are speculative, novelty is not the same as clarity, and cryptic brevity is simple to write but not simple to understand.

title: Separation of concerns
question: What does separation of concerns mean in software design?
options: Splitting a program into parts that each address a distinct concern, such as UI, business rules or data access
Separating the team into groups that never read each other's code to avoid conflicting opinions during reviews
Keeping each concern in a different repository, so that no module is ever allowed to call another module
Placing every function in its own file, regardless of whether the functions relate to the same responsibility
explanation: Separation of concerns divides a system so each part handles one aspect, letting you change or test it without disturbing the others. It does not mean isolating people, forbidding calls between modules, or one file per function; parts still collaborate through clear interfaces.

title: The Boy Scout Rule
question: What does the Boy Scout Rule for code say?
options: Leave the code a little cleaner than you found it each time you work on it
Rewrite every module you open from scratch so that it follows the latest team conventions
Never touch code that works, because any cleanup might introduce a regression nobody asked about
Report each smell in the tracker and wait for a dedicated cleanup sprint before changing anything
explanation: The rule encourages small, continuous improvements, such as a clearer name or a removed duplication, whenever you pass through code, so quality does not erode over time. Wholesale rewrites are risky, refusing to touch working code lets mess accumulate, and waiting only for cleanup sprints postpones small fixes that are cheap now.

title: Fail fast
question: What does the fail-fast principle recommend?
options: Catch every exception at the top level and continue running with default values to keep the system always available
Delay input validation until the data is actually used deep in the program, so that normal flows stay short
Report a problem immediately and visibly at the point it is detected, instead of continuing in a bad state
Optimize each function to run as quickly as possible, so that failures are rare and cheap when they do occur
explanation: Failing fast means stopping with a clear error as soon as something is wrong, such as an invalid argument, so the bug is found near its cause rather than much later as corrupted data. Swallowing errors hides defects, late validation spreads bad state, and performance tuning is unrelated to how failures are surfaced.
